claims.text: Engineered defective carbon supports provide stronger interfacial anchoring for nanoparticles than pristine carbon supports.
Strong interfacial anchoring increases the effective surface cohesive energy of HEA nanoparticles.
Increasing nanoparticle surface cohesive energy delays the onset of premelting and melting.
Standard carbon-based supports have typical defect densities that provide a baseline state for supported HEA nanoparticles.
Controlled thermal treatment can produce highly defective turbostratic graphite supports.
Controlled ion treatment can produce the proposed highly defective T-graphite support.
Comparing otherwise identical nanoparticles on highly defective and minimally defective supports isolates support defect density as the intervention.
Defective T-graphite provides numerous nanoparticle nucleation sites.
Nanoparticles can partially intercalate and anchor at defective graphite edge planes, producing high support-binding energy.
Vacancy clusters in the carbon support enhance interfacial binding to HEA nanoparticles.
Stronger nanoparticle-support binding suppresses surface-atom mobility during heating.
Nanoparticles on engineered defective supports will have higher premelting and melting onset temperatures than nanoparticles on pristine supports.
Nanoparticles on engineered defective supports will undergo less sintering or coalescence during heating than nanoparticles on pristine supports.
Anchoring nanoparticles to defective T-graphite provides enhanced thermal stability.
The proposed mechanism should hold for carbon-supported nanoparticles below approximately 100 nm when interfacial anchoring dominates surface-energy modulation.
The mechanism may be less applicable to nanoparticles with inherently low melting points or when other support-related thermal effects dominate.
The magnitude of any premelting or melting-temperature shift may depend on nanoparticle composition, support defect type and density, and heating rate.
In situ TEM and DSC measurements can jointly determine premelting onset, melting behavior, and heating-induced morphology changes in the proposed comparison.

contradictions.description: The initial state and baseline describe supports with typical or standard defect densities as pristine, whereas the intervention defines the pristine control as minimally defective. This leaves the actual control defect density internally inconsistent.
